en: The Buddha-spoken Mahāvaipulya Mañjuśrī Sūtra.
[Recorded by] the Duke of Su, who held the rank of Kaifu Yitong Sisi, served as Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
was granted three thousand households of fiefdom, bestowed the purple robe, posthumously awarded the title of Sikong, and conferred the posthumous name Dajian (Great Mirror).

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of the Great Xingshan Monastery, Possessor of Great and Vast Wisdom, by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: The Prophecy. The Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. At that time, the World-Honored One...
Again, having surveyed the palaces of the Śuddhāvāsa devas everywhere,
he addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
Because you are able to take pity on many sentient beings,
you abide in the form of a dhāraṇī and expound and establish it for the sake of sentient beings.
Exhorting others to progress and rejoicing in their merit, one understands its underlying principles.
For practitioners, one reveals the essential points of the Dharma and various homa rites;
through skillful means, one is able to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, having attained the fruits of the Two Vehicles, humans, and devas,
they are able to perform various Buddha-works for sentient beings with their purified bodies,
manifesting the body of a Buddha.
He establishes himself in the quiescent nirvana of non-abiding.
If there are sentient beings who should be liberated by means of the body of Maheśvara,
he immediately manifests the body of Maheśvara.
For the sake of those sentient beings, he expounds the secret dharma of dhāraṇīs;
even to the extent that he may manifest in the form of Śakra,
the form of a garuḍa, or the form of a kiṃnara.
Mahoragas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and those with the forms of the sun, moon, and stars;
boys and girls; and various other bodies, including those of diverse species—whether bipeds, quadrupeds, multi-limbed beings, or those without limbs.
For those sentient and insentient beings within the three realms who are to be liberated,
he manifests himself before them all and expounds the Dharma for them.
For this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
At that time, the Blessed One again praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
It is truly rare that you are able to benefit sentient beings through such skillful means,
manifesting various bodies to reveal and expound the teachings.
You are a truly pure bodhisattva.
In a future age, for as many eons as there are atoms in an asaṃkhyeya of worlds,
you shall [dwell] in the world-system called Universal Illumination of Equality.
He shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, titled Equal Radiance Universally Shining.
May those sentient beings abide in fearlessness,
free from all feverish afflictions and without change,
reaching ultimate quiescence.
Only then will he enter the Great Parinirvāṇa. At that time,
after the World-Honored One had bestowed this prediction upon the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and the immeasurable assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas [were filled with joy].
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, they received the light of Universal Radiance that Shines Everywhere;
it illuminated immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions, making them all brilliantly bright.
Among them, those sentient beings who encountered this light...
Swiftly attaining excellent benefit and being freed from all suffering and affliction,
they all resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta;
the entire great assembly then called to mind the body of the Buddha.
Each remained silently in their respective seats.
A rain of various celestial flowers fell and a cool, fragrant breeze spread throughout the great assembly.
At that time, the great multitude [beheld] in the midst of the sky.
Each beheld immeasurable Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
pervading the buddha-fields of the ten directions without exception.
At that time, the great assembly together uttered these words:
"Homage to the Buddha! This is the majestic spiritual power of the World-Honored One.
All those in the assembly, seeing this miraculous transformation, felt joy in their hearts and were freed from all doubt."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat,
circumambulated the Buddha three times,
and prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet; he gazed up at the Tathāgata without blinking for even a moment.
Radiant with a gentle smile and holding a white flower, he stood there with a sincere heart.
At that time, all the Buddhas from the worlds of the ten directions each rained down clouds of various colored flowers.
Within those clouds of flowers were divine, exquisite garments,
flower garlands, golden cords, necklaces, banners,
and *pārijātaka* nets— various articles of adornment.
They filled the entirety of space, covering the Buddha from above, and further produced wondrous sounds, praising him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Today the Tathāgata, for the sake of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara..."
The Great Consecration of the Dharma-Wheel King was performed;
with immeasurable ornaments and sublime voices,
those praised by humans and devas all came forth to appear.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the entire assembly of Bodhisattvas,
those of the six heavens of desire and the realm of form, as well as the stainless Pure Abodes—
those sons of the Buddha who have received the consecration— all have gathered here like clouds.
Koti-millions of māras and many kinds of sentient beings,
all bearing exquisite offerings, come to present them to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
sharing the same vows for the future, may they all become like Avalokiteśvara.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara prostrated at the feet of the Honored One, praised the Tathāgata,
and then returned to his original seat, speaking as follows:
This dhāraṇī was proclaimed, rejoiced in, and authenticated by the Buddhas of the past,
such as Vipaśyin and others, as well as by me, the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
And in the future, the World-Honored One Maitreya and all other Buddhas,
numbering as many as incalculable aeons,
shall likewise proclaim it.
Having spoken these words,
he entered the Samādhi of Universal Radiance Tārā.
By the power of that samādhi,
From the pupil of the right eye on his countenance, he emitted a great radiance;
following the flow of that light, the form of a sublime woman appeared,
abiding in the samādhi of supreme and wondrous color.
Their bodies were adorned with priceless miscellaneous jewels,
like refined pure gold reflecting lapis lazuli;
that is to say, they had accomplished the essentials of the secret mantra of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
It can pacify the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings,
and it can also bring joy to all sentient beings;
it universally enters the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm of all Buddhas.
Abiding in equanimity like space, he universally addresses all sentient beings, saying:
"Who is undergoing transformation and suffering? Who is drowning in the ocean of birth and death?"
"I shall vow to deliver them.
Having spoken these words,
he traveled throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Returning to the place where the Buddha was, he circumambulated him three times to the right,
prostrated with his head at the feet of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
and with palms joined in reverence, held a blue lotus flower.
Gazing up at the Bodhisattva, they remained there receiving his instruction,
contemplating the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual power as he universally illumined all sentient beings with cool, refreshing light.
Just as the cool lunar orb in the world can dispel the heat of affliction and illuminate all darkness so that nothing remains unseen,
he surpassed this even further by containing a playful smile.
He compassionates sentient beings like a loving mother.
With the light of his compassion, he universally illumines the Buddha-fields,
such that the radiance of all the devas becomes entirely invisible.
At that time, the auspicious and pure Avalokiteśvara,
having paid homage to the World-Honored One, spoke these verses:
"Throughout millions of kalpas, I have expounded this Tārā."
The principles, mantras, seasons, and directions—
thus did the Buddhas of the past also extensively proclaim them;
they are as boundless as space, and no one can measure them.
Now, regarding a small portion of this matter, I shall explain it according to its nature:
if a person practices excellently, their supreme vows will all be fulfilled;
throughout the ten directions and for the duration of their lives, there shall be nothing they do not obtain as they wish.
If there are sentient beings who, seeking the fruits of human and celestial realms,
uphold this sublime Dharma and practice according to its teachings for immeasurable *koṭi* eons, they shall experience supreme and wondrous bliss.
If one desires to seek the ten stages and fulfill the rank of a bodhisattva—
The Difficult to Conquer, the Immovable, The Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma—
One should uphold the Honored Tārā, Ten million and three hundred million times.
According to the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties,
If one practices such sublime cultivation for sixteen lakṣas, One will certainly attain the matters described above.
If you wish to see Avalokiteśvara, The auspicious and pure one, [you shall behold him].
If one recites [the mantra] seven hundred thousand times, there is no doubt that one will behold him.
If one seeks to see the Great Being Vimala, the Lord Avalokiteśvara,
and recites it a full ten million times, the Holy One will certainly appear before one.
If, throughout the three periods of the day, one recites with a tranquil mind free from defilement and single-minded devotion,
one will swiftly fulfill the six perfections and realize the Tathāgatagarbha, Nirvāṇa, and the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).
The indestructible body of radiant light, seated upon the vajra throne in the peerless samādhi;
turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma to open the eyes of gods and humans— this is for the sake of practicing Tārā.

As described above, all are fully perfected; those who wish to realize the ritual procedures and various skillful means of the dhāraṇī, the definitive meaning, and the profound principles of the sūtras,
as well as the cessation of the suffering of the three realms of existence— [should practice this].

One should recite it one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*). If one desires to seek Brahmā and Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, or to become a Wheel-Turning King, a Lord of Men, one should complete one hundred thousand recitations.
If one desires to travel to the Snowy Mountains, [one should likewise do so].
And Citikṣaya, Sumeru and Cakravāḍa, Sakhi and Sukhāvatī, Mālā and Sukhadhvaja, Śrī and Abū, Nibū and Kailāsa.
Citrakūṭa and the others, with their variegated and wondrous colors,
as well as Śrī and the pure [realms]— such abodes of sages and seers should all be recited one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*). Yakṣas and Gandharvas.
To the rākṣasa and nāga palaces, and even to the celestial mansions,
one can go at will; resolving all doubts and understanding all matters according to their nature—
one who desires to seek such vows as these [should practice].
One should recite it one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*).
Desiring to enter the palace of the asuras where the kinnaras dwell, one shall summon the yakṣiṇīs,
the vidyādharīs, the nāgakanyās, and the kinnarakanyās.
They shall all come at their thought, playing and enjoying themselves as they please;
seeking the prolongation of life, the medicine of the deathless nectar,
abundant wealth, servants, and all the pleasures of the five senses.
One should recite it one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*).
Even if I and the Tathāgata were to expound its merits for tens of millions (*koṭi*) of eons, we could not exhaust them;
such is the merit of one who upholds this *tārā*.
She who should receive the offerings of gods and humans, the Great Compassionate One,
the Mother of All; since there is not a single god, human, or yakṣa who is not her child, she is called the Mother of the World.
And those who have transcended the world: Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Vajrapāṇi, and Sudhana;
Mañjuśrī, Subhūti, Maitreya, and Gajagandha; Candraprabha and Akṣayamati.
Vimalagaganagañja, Locanā, Mahāmati, and the Bodhisattvas such as Vimalakīrti—
these are all the sons of Tārā and likewise the mothers of Prajñā, as well as the Tathāgatas of the three times.
Among all Mahāsattvas, there is not one who is not my son;
all address me as their mother. Out of compassion, I nurture all sentient beings, supporting them like the great earth.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara, having spoken this verse, [remained silent].
He then spoke this dhāraṇī for the Bodhisattva Tārā:

*Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya. Tadyathā: oṃ tāre tuttare ture svāhā.* When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara had thus spoken the dhāraṇī, [he continued:]
By the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Tārā,
all sentient beings in every world are freed from all suffering and affliction and attain peace and happiness.
They all gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
They were all in accord with the essential nature of the dharma-realm.
They entered the treasury of the gate of birth that is without limit.
The entire assembly felt a sense of wonder in their hearts and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Chapter Two: The Maṇḍala. From the Avalokiteśvara Tārā Bodhisattva Sūtra, Chapter Two: The Maṇḍala. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara...
He addressed the Bodhisattva Tārā, saying:
"If a woman wishes to accomplish all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and desires to fulfill her supreme vows for the world..."
One should practice this essential secret.
Its maṇḍala is exactly like that of the present Tathāgata Śākyamuni in the palace of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
In the assembly where one gathers with the bodhisattvas,
the practitioner should first select a location—
either on a mountain peak or by a riverbank.
Or near the great ocean, by flowers, fruits, springs, and ponds—
in such secluded places, free from all dangers,
as well as from mlecchas, hostile bandits, and venomous insects.
In a place of impurity such as that of a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcasts,
measure out a space of four, eight, or even sixteen cubits.
Dig a pit one cubit deep and remove all bones, hair, ashes, charcoal, thorns, and other impure substances.
Take soil from the riverbank and various pure soils;
having first sprinkled them with the five purifiers,
recite the mantra of the tutelary deity one hundred and eight times.
He consecrated the soil to fill the ground,
clearing and leveling it until it was perfectly smooth.
He then took the dung of a yellow cow that had not fallen to the ground.
Having also recited the dhāraṇī to empower it,
one should then smear the ground on an auspicious month and under a favorable lunar mansion.
Alternatively, on the fifteenth day of the first month, the eighth day of the second month, the fifteenth day of the second month,
and so forth, one should begin at night and empower the site of the maṇḍala with the blue lotus mudrā.
Take five-colored silken threads to mark out the boundary lines;
use five-colored powders to knead and draw them,
or prepare seven-jeweled powders according to one's means.
Mix with various powdered incenses and recite the dhāraṇī.
For the four directions and three enclosures,
first paint Śākyamuni Buddha in the central womb.
Seated upon a precious lion throne in the posture of preaching the Dharma,
one should depict to his right the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara seated upon a lotus flower,
gazing up with palms joined and holding a white lotus.
His body is white with a reddish hue, adorned with necklaces and ornaments;
he wears a jeweled crown on his head and a white divine cord draped over his left shoulder.
To his left, one should paint the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
Holding a vajra in his left hand, his body is light green.
Following this, one should paint the eight great bodhisattvas,
namely Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
and Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin,
and the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.
Below the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha,
one should further depict the Bodhisattva Trailokyavijaya Vidyārāja.
One should assume a wrathful form and paint the wrathful Bodhisattva Candrānanā,
making the gesture of clenching the fists to crush and subdue all māras.
Near Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
paint Bhūkuṭī and the White-Robed Avalokiteśvara.
The Hayagrīva Vidyārāja [are] each according to their respective colors,
positioned near the Bodhisattva Hayagrīva.
Paint Mahāśrī Avalokiteśvara, Mahāśvetā Avalokiteśvara,
and Candraprabha Avalokiteśvara.
The Avalokiteśvara of Abundant Wealth and the Avalokiteśvara of Renown [sat] beneath the lion throne of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Paint a lotus pond. Within that pond, there is a wondrous jewel lotus,
crimson in color like red crystal, emitting great radiance.
Seated upon that lotus is the Bodhisattva Tārā;
her left hand holds a blue lotus,
and her right hand is placed palm-upward at her navel in the posture of meditative concentration.
The eye is also like this:
adorned with necklaces and ornaments, and draped in gauze and robes of the morning glow,
it remains there with a serene countenance.
The four gates of that altar were adorned with banners, streamers, and flower canopies;
it featured railings, steps, balustrades, *nandikas*, and conch shells,
while the various devas played music and chanted praises for the assembly of sages.
On the eastern side of the altar, paint the host of Akaniṣṭha devas,
including the son of heaven Parīttābha and the son of heaven Atapa.
On the northern side, depict the devaputra Sudarśana and the devaputra Supratiṣṭhita;
on both sides of the gate, depict Brahmā and the Brahmakāyika devas.
In each of the four directions, paint two deities from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and the Mahābrahmā Heaven;
all of them wear jeweled crowns and are clad in crimson robes.
Some were yellow and some were white, their bodies unadorned with necklaces;
they remained seated in meditation,
each placing their right hand upon the crown of their head in the gesture of respectful salutation.
On the side of the outer courtyard gate,
one should paint the Māra king Kṛṣṇapāṇḍu,
adorned with jeweled necklaces and possessing the appearance of a youth.
Next, paint the gods of Nirmāṇarati, Tuṣita, Yāma, and Śakra-devendra,
who stand near the gate. Next,
paint the Four Heavenly Kings, the Garuḍa gods, and Īśāna, the lord of spirits.
And depict Viṣṇu standing while holding a wheel;
next, depict the great yakṣa general Pañcika;
next, depict the great yakṣa Lambaka.
And [the yakṣa kings] Pūrṇabhadra and Ratnabhadra; and the great yakṣiṇī Hārītī;
and the four sisters who are the sun, moon, and lunar mansions.
The youth Ghaṭikāra, along with the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda,
and all such noble beings must be invited with single-minded devotion and dispatched with the mind.
Take white flowers and place them within an *argha* bowl.
Offer them to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all mantra-siddhas.
Both worldly and world-transcending beings must be visualized completely and offered to with a sincere heart.
Prepare scented water using white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron,
and sprinkle it over the assembly of noble ones.
Furthermore, grind these same fragrances into powder and burn them as incense.
When these words have been spoken,
one should pray: "I beseech all Buddhas, all great Bodhisattvas, and all holy beings to grant me siddhi,
and to cause me to swiftly emerge from the mire of birth and death."
Having recited this three times,
one should perform offerings according to what one's means permit,
while constantly keeping in mind and invoking all the worldly and world-transcending mantra-deities.
"May you grant me your empowerment.
Forming each of their respective root mudrās in conjunction with this,
one fills eight new vases with scented water.
Place all types of seeds and the seven treasures, gold, and silver;
as well as various medicinal herbs, branches of the āmalaka tree,
and leaves of willow, nyagrodha, pine, and cypress.
Tie uncut silk ribbons over the mouths of the jars.
Place four jars at the four inner corners and four jars at the four outer corners.
Furthermore, place eight vases:
the first vase is for making offerings to the assembly of the Akaniṣṭha devas of the form realm;
the second vase is for making offerings to the assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
The third bottle is for making offerings to the devas of the desire realm;
the fourth bottle is for making offerings to the yakṣas, devīs, and vidyādhara sages;
the fifth bottle is for making offerings to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
The sixth bottle is offered to the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
The seventh bottle is offered before the Tārā.
The eighth bottle is offered to all sentient beings.
In this manner, all six vases must be arranged one by one according to the ritual rules.
At each of the four sides of the maṇḍala, a ghee lamp shall be lit.
The unguents, incense, flower garlands, and exquisite foods—
each according to the ritual of the Mañjuśrī Maṇḍala—
are all consecrated with the dhāraṇī of the central deity.
Four or five cubits from the southwest corner of the mandala,
one should perform the homa of Guṇḍarī;
its hearth should be square with four corners.
It may be one cubit, two cubits, or half a cubit deep;
within the hearth, a lotus shape should be fashioned.
The hearth should be excavated according to the method for selecting the site.
Take newly drilled pure fire and use wood from milky trees as fuel.
Take all kinds of grasses, flowers, and the five seeds,
and mix them with ghee, honey, and curd.
First, offer three ladles of clarified butter to the fire deity and burn them.
Next, offer three ladles each of honey and curd.
Then, place three of the five seeds into the fire.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ agni svāhā. Recite this secret mantra to empower it.
Then, take white sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and other such substances, and mix them with scented water.
Place [the offerings] in vessels made of clay, wood, gold, silver, or refined copper that are new and pure, and set them to the right side.
Having invited the Fire Deity (Agni),
take flowers and incense, recite the root dhāraṇī, and cast them into the fire as an offering to the Fire Deity.
With the right hand, take scented water and sprinkle it clockwise upon the fire while employing the root ritual (*mūla-vidhi*).
First, protect yourself;
next, form the blue lotus mudrā, visualize the Bodhisattva Tārā, and recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times. Then, take various white flowers and place them in *argha* water.
Visualizing the deity, hold [the vessel] and make offerings.
First, pour out three drops.
Then take white sandalwood, saffron, and camphor.
Mix together ghee, honey, and curd. Then,
take wood from a milky tree that is free of knots, straight,
and twelve finger-widths long, cutting it into one thousand and eight pieces.
Recite the mantra once and cast [the offering] into the fire pit each time;
once it has been burned, the Bodhisattva Tārā will manifest her form and say to the practitioner:
"What wish do you seek? I shall grant you everything."
Even if a practitioner has accumulated heavy karmic obstructions,
[the deity] will manifest warnings,
either by emitting light or by causing sounds such as thunder, bells, and gongs to be heard.
Either rain falls from a cloudless sky, or a fragrant,
cool, and wondrous breeze touches the practitioner’s body;
having encountered such auspicious signs, they give rise to great joy and exultation.
When the hosts of devas and humans see the practitioner, they will give rise to joy in their hearts.
One should know that the Bodhisattva Tārā will soon fulfill his vows.
This is true if the ācārya performs this rite for him.
Having dismissed the assembly of noble ones and offered the *argha* water,
one should immediately recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times at the site of practice as usual,
circumambulate it three times, and perform walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) as desired.
Recite the mantra for one's own fundamental vow three times daily,
or for one week, two weeks, or even up to three weeks.
Having completed the recitation,
one should take the water from the offering vessel before the deity Tārā Bodhisattva,
form the blue lotus mudrā, and sprinkle it upon the crown of the practitioner’s head.
At the site of the consecration,
eight cubits from the mandala, one should draw a lotus flower;
having performed the consecration, one should circumambulate it three times.
Once again offer argha water and recite various hymns of praise.
Form the mudrā of the principal deity and place a white lotus upon it;
scatter these over the maṇḍala as an offering.
Thereafter, perform the dismissal as is customary.
Place the flower-powder from within the maṇḍala into pure flowing water;
one must not step upon it.
Furthermore, the site of the maṇḍala should be smeared with cow dung.
As for the offerings of food and drink, they should be bestowed upon the community of monks and the poor.
Those who have previously entered the maṇḍala and practiced therein should not consume this.
One must also not eat eggplant, radish, or the roots and stalks of the lotus;
nor must one step upon the shadow of a stūpa, the shadow of an ācārya or one's parents, or the shadow of a pure bhikṣu who is a practitioner.
Furthermore, one must not step upon the shadows of the Bodhi trees of even the seven Buddhas.
Chapter Three: The Chapter on Painted Images from the Avalokiteśvara Tārā Bodhisattva Sūtra. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha...
Furthermore, he observed the palaces of the Śuddhāvāsa deities and addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"You should now, in turn, explain the method for painting images for the Bodhisattva Tārā."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
receiving the holy command of the Buddha, rose from his seat,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and then surveyed the palaces of the Śuddhāvāsa deities all around.
And he commanded the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas,
as well as all the vidyādharas and mantra-siddha ṛṣis of the entire world.
He made this vow:
"You all should listen to and remember this samaya; do not give rise to doubt.
In future ages, those who practice should provide protection."
If you give rise to a contrary thought, the Great Yakṣa General Vajrapāṇi will shatter the crown of your head with his vajra-flame-tipped mallet;
at the end of your life, you shall fall into hell.
They shall undergo great suffering and affliction for immeasurable kalpas.
At that time, having finished his vow, the Bodhisattva addressed the Bodhisattva Tārā, saying: "If there are practitioners in future ages..."
When seeking to attain the supreme siddhi of perfection,
one should paint an image according to my instructions and the Dharma,
using fresh white cotton cloth or various silks that have not been cut into panels.
The assembly must be pure and free of body hair; the flowers and pigments must be fresh and clean.
One should select the most skilled artist and those who have generated the bodhicitta and possess a fully prepared physical vessel to receive the eight precepts of the upavāsa.
It may be eight cubits, four cubits, or even one cubit in size. First,
within the central platform, one should paint Śākyamuni Bhagavān seated upon a lion throne made of various jewels, situated within a palace of the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
The body is golden in color and displays the gesture of preaching the Dharma.
To the left, one should paint the youth Mañjuśrī,
adorned with necklaces and ornaments, with a slightly reddish hue.
She wears a skirt of blue silk and a light gauze robe,
bound with divine cords;
her right hand holds a white whisk, and her left hand grasps the stem of a blue lotus.
He stands gazing upward.
To the right is painted the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
his body light red in color, with hair adorned by a jeweled crown containing an emanation Buddha.
Wearing a white divine cord (*devasūtra*),
he sits in the *utkuṭaka* posture upon a lotus.
His left hand holds a lotus, and his right hand is raised above his head in the gesture of scattering flowers.
Adorning their bodies with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments,
they should display a smiling countenance;
next, one should likewise paint the Bodhisattva Tārā.
Adorned with priceless miscellaneous jewels,
his body is greenish-yellow in color like that of a person in the prime of youth;
he gazes upon the practitioner with a compassionate smile.
He stands bowing toward Avalokiteśvara;
his left hand holds a blue lotus, and his right hand makes the gesture of grasping an auspicious fruit.
Below the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...
One should depict the practitioner holding an incense burner in the posture of prostration.
To the right of the seat, one should draw a golden bowl filled with ripe āmalaka fruits.
In the lower section, depict the devaputras Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Sudarśana,
in the posture of listening to the Dharma.
In the upper section, on the right side, depict the devaputra Akaniṣṭha.
On the left, depict the Devaputra Subhūti;
his right hand scatters flowers and his left hand performs the gesture of salutation.
Above, depict jeweled canopies and the musical performances of the devas.
The four sides of the empty space are entirely painted with dragon-flowers (*nāgapuṣpa*).
If a practitioner makes offerings with utmost sincerity and prostrates once,
they shall extinguish the sins of birth and death accumulated over billions of kalpas.
Chapter Two: The Second Illustrated Image of the Bodhisattva Tārā. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Bodhisattva Tārā, saying:
If a practitioner further wishes to accomplish the second method of painting an image,
they should first paint Amitāyus Buddha in the central platform,
leaning against a bodhi tree.
On the left is painted the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhā, white in color, adorned with various ornaments and wearing fine gauze garments;
she holds a white fly-whisk and gazes askance toward the Buddha.
On the right is painted the four-armed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The right hand performs the *abhaya-mudrā*;
with the middle finger and thumb, it holds a rosary,
while the hand is extended in the gesture of stroking the head (*mūrdha-sparśana*).
The second right hand forms the gesture of holding a staff;
the first left hand holds a red lotus flower,
and the second left hand holds a *kamaṇḍalu*.
To the right of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
depict the Bodhisattva Tārā with a body adorned with exquisite jewels, greenish-yellow in color,
with palms joined and holding a blue lotus flower.
Sitting in the half-lotus posture,
he assumes an air of reverent bowing.
Bodhisattva Vigatarajas descends.
Paint the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī with three eyes and four arms.
Her body is clad in white garments;
her first left hand holds a lotus flower, and her second left hand holds a *kamaṇḍalu*.
The right hand performs the *abhaya-mudrā* (gesture of fearlessness), and the second hand holds a rosary.
Below the Bodhisattva Tārā,
paint a single-tufted rākṣasa.
His eyes were blackish-red and his belly hung down;
he wore snakes as a necklace, with dog-teeth protruding from his upper jaw;
he donned a tiger-skin skirt, and great pythons coiled around his hair.
His right hand holds a battle-axe and his left hand grasps a snake-noose;
his body is smeared with blood.
With both hands joined in *añjali*, he knits his brows and glares with wrathful eyes, manifesting a terrifying appearance.
The fingernails are slender and sharp, with webbed fingers like those of an elephant. Below Bījakṛti,
paint the four-armed Hayagrīva Bodhisattva.
Form the root mudrā with both hands:
hold a battle-axe in the right hand and grasp a lotus in the left.
Stand in the *ting* posture and assume a wrathful expression.
Beneath the image, Nanda and Upananda, the Dragon Kings, are depicted;

their left hands hold lotus stalks, while their right hands are in the gesture of salutation. Below the pond, the Earth Goddess (Pṛthivīdevatā) is painted, kneeling with one knee on the ground, holding a jeweled platter and gazing up in reverence.
In the four cardinal directions and four intermediate corners, paint the deities of the eight directions.
Above, paint the sun and moon, the various devas, and celestial music.
Amidst five-colored clouds, depict the appearance of sweet rain falling.
Below Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one should paint the practitioner wearing white robes, holding an incense burner, and kneeling with legs drawn up in reverence while gazing upward.
If a practitioner, on the eighth or fifteenth day of the month, or during a month of supernatural powers (*ṛddhimāsa*), [performs this practice...]
Alternatively, when the lunar mansions are auspicious,
one should consume milk porridge, flowers, fruits, and other such foods;
or one may consume only fragrances.
Following the previously established rules for recitation, one should bathe at the three times of day and must not sleep.
One should always sit upon *kuśa* grass, wearing white garments.
When the prescribed number of days is nearly completed, one should abstain from food for three days.
Perform infinite recitations before this image.
Place scented water at each of the four corners of the maṇḍala;
in the vases, insert leaves from various fragrant trees such as the *nyagrodha* and the willow.
One should also place seven treasures and seeds of the five grains [within the vases],
using uncut silken cloths to cover the mouths of the vases.
The practitioner sits at a table to the left side.
Place the Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā sūtra upon the altar and scatter flowers over it.
In the eight directions, place eight pure vessels, each filled with scented water.
Furthermore, set out eight bowls of milk,
light one hundred butter lamps,
and place various kinds of food and drink in new vessels.
Place incense burners at the four corners of the altar and burn aloeswood incense.
Kindle a fire of milky wood and take twelve-finger-length pieces of aloeswood, cutting them into one hundred and eight segments.
Burn one drop of storax resin incense for every recitation, completing one hundred and eight repetitions.
Then the Noble One, the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
will come from the eastern direction.
Holding a staff in his hand and wearing white garments,
he was adorned with exquisite jewel necklaces;
he wore a black antelope skin draped across his right shoulder.
Wearing a jeweled crown upon his hair,
he manifests a great radiance before those who practice,
universally illuminating the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
When sentient beings afflicted by suffering have passed through this light,
their bodies become peaceful and joyful, and they give rise to the bodhicitta.
Upon seeing this, the practitioner scatters various flowers and incense.
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground,
one should take refuge with utmost sincerity and offer *argha* water to the Bodhisattva.
Then, the Greatly Compassionate Holy One, Avalokiteśvara, will speak to the practitioner, saying:
"Excellent! O practitioners, what is your wish?
I shall grant you everything.
Having received this authorization, whatever the heart desires will be accomplished without exception.
Some may fly through the void, or attain *ādhāraṇa* (mastery); some may gain the power of hearing and retaining teachings or prolong their lifespan;
and some whose faculties were incomplete may likewise attain perfection.
Or they may seek hidden treasures and enter the caves of the asuras;
they shall likewise be able to enter at will the palace of Avalokiteśvara.
All such supreme aspirations shall be fulfilled.
There is nothing, whether mundane or supramundane, that will not be accomplished.
Furthermore, recite this secret mantra to bid farewell to the noble one.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:

*Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo ’ryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya. Hiri hiri sulu sulu sarvasattvakaṭuṇika jeṣa jeṣaya. Aryāvalokiteśvarāya te samayam anuprasara svāhā.* The practitioner should hold various incenses and flowers.
Recite this mantra seven times to perform the consecration;
then, scattering [the flowers] at the feet of the Bodhisattva, one accomplishes the dispatching [of the deity]. The Dhāraṇī of the Single-Tufted Rākṣasī is as follows:

Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo ’ryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya. Namo vikarālāya mahāṛkṣi asyāramama mahāṛkṣi mamamukha sarvakāriṇi karohi. Tadyathā: ānandi svāhā, jayaye svāhā, sarvavidyāvinayanaya kṣa kṣa svāhā. This dhāraṇī enables one to achieve accomplishment swiftly with little effort.
He is also the messenger of the Bodhisattva Tārā;
therefore, all practitioners of the path should recite and keep him in mind.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the Mahāvaipulya Mañjuśrī Sūtra.
